value: two-sided limit does NOT exist: right-hand limit = 0 (2^(1/x) -> +inf so 3 - 2^(1/x) -> -inf), left-hand limit = 1/3 (2^(1/x) -> 0)
why: sympy gives lim_{x->0+} = 0 and lim_{x->0-} = 1/3, corroborated numerically at 60 dps (x=+1e-6 gives -1e-301030, x=-1e-6 gives 0.3333...), so the two-sided limit does not exist and no option states that. Both one-sided values are printed as options (A = 0 is the right-hand limit, D = 1/3 is the left-hand limit), which is exactly the shape of a question whose key picked one branch; A (=0) is the likelier intended key since the 2^(1/x) -> inf branch is the one such items usually intend.

value: f is continuous exactly at the points x = k*pi (k integer), and nowhere else
why: Approaching a along irrationals gives 0 and along rationals gives sin|a|, so continuity at a forces sin|a| = 0, i.e. a = k*pi; at every such a (a=0 rational with f(0)=0, a=k*pi irrational with f(a)=0) both limits and the value are 0, so f really is continuous there. A and B are false and C asserts the opposite of what holds at k*pi.

|x sin(pi/x)| <= |x| -> 0, and sympy confirms lim_{x->0} x sin(pi/x) = 0, so the only value making f continuous at 0 is 0; option D ('all of these') would require -1 and 1 to work too, which they do not.

2x/(1+3x^2) = (3x - x)/(1 + 3x*x) with product 3x^2 >= 0 > -1, so the first term is arctan(3x) - arctan(x) for every real x, giving 3/(1+9x^2) - 1/(1+x^2); the second term differentiates to 26/((1-5x)^2+(5+x)^2) = 1/(1+x^2), which cancels the -1/(1+x^2). sympy simplifies the whole derivative to 3/(9x^2+1) and matches only option B (checked at x = 1/2, 2, -3/7, where all four options take distinct exact values).

At x = -10 both x-2 and x+1 are negative, so locally f(x) = (2-x) + (-x-1) - x = 1 - 3x, a straight line of slope -3; sympy's derivative and an exact rational symmetric difference quotient both return -3.
(1+x^2)y1 = 2 arctan x; differentiating gives (1+x^2)y2 + 2x y1 = 2/(1+x^2), and multiplying by (1+x^2) yields (x^2+1)^2 y2 + 2x(x^2+1) y1 = 2. sympy simplifies the expression to the constant 2.

From (1-x^2)y2 - x y1 = a^2 y, n-fold Leibniz differentiation gives (1-x^2)y_{n+2} - (2n+1)x y_{n+1} = (n(n-1) + n + a^2) y_n = (n^2 + a^2) y_n; sympy computed the ratio lhs/y_n symbolically at n = 0,1,2,3 and returned a^2, a^2+1, a^2+4, a^2+9 exactly.

f'(x) = 6(x+2)(x-1) < 0 exactly on (-2,1) (sympy solveset). Checking each option's midpoint: f' = -12 at x=0 (option C) but +81/2, +21/2, +21/2 at the midpoints of A, B and D, so no other option is even partly a decreasing interval.
f(x) expands to 5x^2 - 30x + 55 with f'' = 10 > 0 and the unique critical point x = 3; exact values f(3)=10 < f(5/2)=45/4 < f(2)=15 < f(5)=30 confirm 3 is the minimiser.

value: f(x) = e^{2x} (any function with f' = 2f, i.e. f = A e^{2x})
why: Differentiating the given identity gives f = f'/2, i.e. f' = 2f, whose general solution is C1 e^{2x}. Testing each option exactly: f' - 2f is 0 only for D; for A and C it equals -2C (so they hold only in the degenerate C = 0 case) and for B it is -2C - 2x + 1.

Multiplying J's integrand by e^{4x}/e^{4x} gives e^{3x}/(e^{4x}+e^{2x}+1), so with t = e^x, J - I = int (t^2-1)/(t^4+t^2+1) dt = int du/(u^2-1) with u = t + 1/t, giving (1/2)log((t^2-t+1)/(t^2+t+1)). sympy differentiated all four options and only C's derivative equals the J-I integrand exactly (A and D differ by a non-zero rational function; B is the negative of C).

Adding the integral to its x -> -x image gives 2I = int_{-pi}^{pi} cos^2 x dx = pi, so I = pi/2 independently of a. mpmath quadrature at 60 dps returns 1.570796326794896619231322 for a = 2, 3, 0.5 and 10, matching pi/2 to 25 digits.

The parabola and the line meet only at (1,2), so the bounded region is the standard one closed off by the y-axis: int_0^2 (y^2/4) dy = 2/3, equivalently int_0^1 (2 - 2 sqrt x) dx = 2/3 (both computed exactly by sympy). The complementary piece under the parabola is 4/3, which is not among the options, so 2/3 is the only reading that lands on an option.

value: degree 1 (the DE is [(1+x) - sqrt(1+x)] y' = 1 + y, linear in y')
why: Solving the curve for a gives a = (sqrt(1+x)-1)/sqrt(1+y) and differentiating gives a = sqrt(1+y)/(sqrt(1+x) y'); eliminating a yields sqrt(1+x)(sqrt(1+x)-1) y' - (1+y) = 0, which sympy reports as degree 1 in y'. The surviving sqrt(1+x) involves only the independent variable and so does not affect the degree.

The family is y^2 = 4ax (a > 0); differentiating gives 2y y' = 4a, and substituting 4a back gives y^2 = 2xy y', i.e. y^2 - 2xy y' = 0. sympy's elimination returns y(y - 2x y') = 0. A one-parameter family needs a first-order equation, which also rules out C and D.
